title: Matplotlib Get Started: Figures and Axes
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and main concepts of Matplotlib Get Started: Figures and Axes.
Create a Matplotlib Figure and Axes suitable for the visualization task.
Apply the relevant plotting API and configure its key properties.
Inspect plotted artists or chart properties to verify the intended result.
Choose labels and visual encodings that communicate data accurately.
prerequisites: NumPy arrays and basic numeric data

understand.concept: A basic Matplotlib workflow imports pyplot, creates a Figure and Axes, adds data, configures labels and renders or saves the result. Explicit Figure and Axes references make programs easier to test and compose.
understand.whyItMatters: A predictable setup prevents charts from leaking state between operations and makes multi-chart programs maintainable.
understand.analogy: Create the page, choose the chart area, add the drawing, then export the finished page.
understand.summary: Matplotlib Get Started: Figures and Axes is part of the Matplotlib learning path. The examples use deterministic data and the Agg backend for automated execution.

explain.narrative: Read the concept, execute each example in sequence, inspect the printed result and compare it with the expected output. Each example creates a figure with the non-interactive Agg backend and closes it after inspection.

examples.title: Create a Figure explicitly
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig = plt.figure()
print(plt.gcf() is fig)
plt.close(fig)

examples.title: Create one Axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
print(len(fig.axes))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A standard subplots call creates one Axes.

examples.title: Create two side-by-side Axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
print(len(axes))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: The axes array contains two plotting areas.

examples.title: Configure a title
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set_title('Monthly sales')
print(ax.get_title())
plt.close(fig)

examples.title: Close a figure cleanly
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
number = fig.number
plt.close(fig)
print(number not in plt.get_fignums())
examples.explanation: Closing figures releases pyplot's reference to them.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small program demonstrating matplotlib get started: figures and axes. Use a deterministic dataset, configure the relevant chart properties, and print at least one check that verifies the result.
practise.independentTask: Apply the technique to a small dataset of your own. Include meaningful labels, check input lengths and explain why the chosen chart is appropriate.
hints: Start with a small deterministic dataset.
Create the Figure and Axes explicitly with plt.subplots().
Inspect the relevant artist or Axes property instead of relying on visual output alone.
Add labels and units that accurately describe the data.
Close figures after automated checks or file export.
practise.challenge: Build a reusable plotting function that validates its inputs, creates the requested chart, and returns or saves a well-labelled Figure without leaking open figures.
validationCriteria: All five examples execute under the pinned Python and Matplotlib environment and match expected output.
Examples use the intended Matplotlib API correctly.
The chart type and visual encodings match the data semantics.
Labels, legends and scales are accurate and readable where applicable.
Figures are closed after automated execution.
